newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FOCUS-Malaysia stock watchdog seen flexing muscle.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Malaysia stock watchdog seen flexing muscle.

text.p: Malaysia's Securities Commission (SC) is signalling that it aims to discipline a market that is competing with its neighbours for foreign funds, analysts said on Wednesday.
On Monday, the market watchdog initiated its first prosecution in court since it was established in early 1993.
It charged Choo Chin Thye, chief executive officer of Repco Holdings Bhd, with making a misleading statement to the Kuala Lumpur Stock Exchange. He pleaded not guilty.

Choo's signature appeared on a January 27, 1996, profit forecast sent by the timber and gaming concern to the Kuala Lumpur Stock Exchange, based on the assumption that authorities would approve its acquisition of a gaming firm. Repco later withdrew the forecast and resubmitted it with lower figures.
Second Board company Repco was once a punter's favourite, rising as much as 2,000 percent last year.
The Second Board index of small-cap stocks has itself more than doubled this year to 635.84 from 298.66 at the end of 1995 on speculative buying, analysts said.
While Repco's stock ended on Tuesday down 5.50 at 80.50 ringgit, it closed up 3.50 at 84.00 ringgit on Wednesday.

"There's pressure for Malaysia to establish itself as a clean, regulated market," said a research chief at a foreign stockbrokerage. "The SC is the great hope for the market as far as that is concerned, and it's beginning to prove it has the authority to do that."
Malaysia is liberalising its markets to better compete in the region against the likes of Singapore and Hong Kong.

Patrick Zecha, head of research at South Johor Securities said: "This (Repco action) adds more credibility or gives the assurance that the Securities Commission and other regulators are doing something within their confines."
The SC has publicly rapped companies in the past for various infractions, but some market watchers say the agency has sometimes moved slowly.
"The SC is keen on being seen as a proper watchdog," said the head of the Kuala Lumpur branch of a foreign brokerage house. "Repco was an easy target."

Previous actions taken by the SC include a 1995 pre-dawn raid on Malaysian Issuing House Sdn Bhd, a stock balloting firm, after being tipped off about alleged irregularities in the balloting of Great Wall Industries Bhd's shares.
Investigators found sacks of unballoted share applications, and later ordered a reballot of the issue. Malaysian Issuing was slapped with a one million ringgit ($400,000) fine.
While the SC's latest action suggests it is taking a tough line, analysts said it has had difficulty in proving its cases and taming a stubborn streak of speculation within the market.

Noting that the Second Board index continued rising on Tuesday following the Repco news, Faez Khairuddin, chief analyst at SJ Securities said: "It would have sent ripples down the investment community, but that's not to say it's actually applied the brakes on sentiment."
"So far as the Second Board is concerned, it (the Repco prosecution) is a blip," he added.
